prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: In 1330, near Siena , a priest was summoned to bring Holy Communion to a gravely ill peasant.
Rather than carry the consecrated Host properly in a pyx, he slipped it irreverently between his breviary’s pages.
He then set out for the sick man’s home.
Arriving at the peasant's bedside and hearing his confession, the priest opened his breviary to retrieve the Host for Communion.
He found it gone, replaced by two round stains of living blood that had soaked through both facing pages exactly where it had been placed.
Shaken and repentant, the priest went at once to the Augustinian priory in Siena to seek guidance from Fr. Simone Fidati of Cascia , a respected holy man.
Fr. Simone heard his confession, granted absolution, and kept the two stained pages of the breviary.
He placed one in a tabernacle at Perugia and carried the other to the Augustinian monastery in his own hometown, Cascia .

The relic kept at Cascia has been examined and documented across the centuries, formally confirmed by Pope Boniface IX in 1389, and the Communal Statutes of Cascia from 1387 already ordered an annual Corpus Christi procession in its honor.
Held up to a light from behind, the bloodstain on the parchment is said to reveal the outline of a bearded human face, a secondary detail noted by generations of pilgrims examining the relic.
The relic remains preserved today in the lower chapel of the Basilica of St. Rita in Cascia.
The town is now more widely known as the home of the fourteenth-century saint St. Rita , whose own shrine draws far larger crowds than the small stained page kept beneath it.

Multiple popes have promoted its veneration since, and the anniversary of the miracle, still marked each year, will reach its seventh centenary in 2030 — a relic born of ordinary carelessness that has now outlasted seven hundred years.
